## Methods

Cases election and material extraction
Ethical approval for the use of these samples and associated data was obtained by a local committee at the institution of origin and via Research Governance at the Wellcome Sanger Institute. This study is part of a larger study that has been approved by the National Health Service Health Research Authority (Research Ethics Committee reference 21/PR/1024, IRAS project ID 304621).

The samples (SA (n=102 primary tumours), SM (n=92 primary tumours), SC-E (n=49 primary tumours and n=1 metastasis), and SC-O (n=26 primary tumours, n=2 recurrences and n=7 metastases), SH (n=6) and KA with sebaceous differentiation (n=1)) were identified from eleven clinical centres across six countries. Representative haematoxylin & eosin (HE)-stained sections were independently reviewed by two specialist dermatopathologists to confirm diagnoses and identify areas for sampling (tumour+/−normal tissue). Immunohistochemistry stains were also reviewed when possible or were performed to aid diagnosis. Clinical data and follow-up were obtained from patient records in keeping with ethical approvals.

All tumour and normal tissue samples were obtained from formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks by either using a tissue microarray (TMA) coring needle or macrodissecting unstained 10-micron thick tissue sections attached to glass slides to collect specifically identified tumour and normal material following a detailed assessment of the H&E slide of each case. Genomic DNA and RNA was extracted from the tumour samples (with genomic DNA only extracted from normal samples) using the AllPrep DNA/RNA FFPE Kit (Qiagen), according to the manufacturer’s instructions.

Sequencing and data processing
Whole exome. Sequencing libraries were prepared from the FFPE-extracted DNA using a NEBNext Ultra II DNA Library Prep Kit (New England Biolabs), according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Unique dual index tags were applied, and the samples were amplified by PCR using the KAPA HiFi Kit (KAPA Biosystems) for a minimum of eight cycles. The libraries were quantified using Accuclear dsDNA Quantitation Kit (Biotium), pooled (8-plex) in an equimolar fashion and hybridised overnight with the SureSelect Human All Exon V5 baits (Agilent). The multiplexed samples were paired-end sequenced using the HiSeq and NovaSeq platforms (Illumina) to generate 101bp reads. Sequencing reads were aligned to the GRCh38 reference genome, using BWA-MEM50, and PCR duplicates were marked using Biobambam2 bammarkduplicates2 (v2.0.146). Tumour-normal sample concordance as well as cross-individual contamination was assessed using Conpair v0.251. Samples were excluded on the basis of quality issues, such as <80% of the targeted regions covered with 20X coverage or more, excessively small library insert size, or cross-individual contamination >5% in either the tumour or normal.

Transcriptome. The FFPE-extracted RNA samples were transcribed, and sequencing libraries prepared using the NEBNext Ultra II Directional RNA Library Prep kit (New England Biolabs) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Unique dual index tags were applied, and the samples were amplified by PCR using the KAPA HiFi HotStart ReadyMix PCR Kit (Roche) for a minimum of 16 cycles. The libraries were quantified using Accuclear dsDNA Quantitation Kit (Biotium), pooled (8-plex) in an equimolar fashion and hybridised overnight with the SureSelect Human All Exon V5 baits (Agilent). The multiplexed samples were paired-end sequenced using the NovaSeq platform (Illumina) to generate 101bp reads. Reads were aligned using STAR v2.5.0c1552 against the GRCh38 human reference genome alongside Ensembl v103 gene annotation. Expression was assessed by counting reads using HTseq v0.7.253 with the appropriate stranded parameter and subsequently transformed into transcripts per million (TPM). Data quality was assessed by running RNA-SeqQC254 and looking at the total number of counts obtained per sample. We discarded any samples that reported: low expression profiling efficiency <40%, 3 prime bias <0.3 or 3 prime bias >0.5, proportion of reads intersecting rRNAs >2.5, read pairs counted <20×107, had higher number of low quality, ambiguous, alignment not unique than reads counted; or number of genes with five counts or more <14×10355.

Analyses
Whole exome
Somatic variant calling. Somatic point mutations were identified using cgpCaVEMan (v1.15.1)56. SmartPhase (v1.2.1)57 was used to identify MNVs from SNVs called with cgpCaVEMan, while adjacent SNVs were first extracted from VCFs generated by CaVEMan. In addition, indels on the autosomes and chromosomes X and Y were identified using cgpPindel (v.3.10.0)58 (https://github.com/cancerit/cgpPindel). For both cgpCaVEMan and cgpPindel, tumours without a matched normal tissue sample were analysed using a BAM file containing ∼50x exome coverage of simulated 100-bp paired-end sequencing reads with an average 300bp insert size generated from the GRCh38 reference genome sequence, without mismatches.

Gene models and the Variant Effect Predictor (VEP)39 from Ensembl v103 were used to predict the consequences of base changes and indels on proteins. The canonical transcript, as defined in Ensembl, was used to determine the variant consequence. VEP was also used to add custom annotations from the COSMIC (v97)59, ClinVar (update 20230121)40, gnomAD (v3.1.2)60 and dbSNP (v155)61 databases. Common SNVs, defined as variants present in 1% or more of the total population in the gnomAD database or the 1000 Genomes Phase 3 dataset (as indicated by dbSNP v155), were excluded as germline variants. Pindel calls were further refined by retaining only variants with VAF≥0.1 and multinucleotide variants of length 3bp or less. Variants were retained where both the reference allele and alternative allele are ≤25bp in length and both alleles are not >10bp, otherwise the variants were retained only if the tumour VAF >0.25 and sequencing coverage at the variant site was ≥20 in both the tumour and matched normal. Finally, variants within 100bp of exome targeted regions and not flagged by cgpCaVEMan or cgpPindel filters were taken forward for further analysis. For the generation of the oncoplots, the FLAG genes were not included as they are frequently found to bear rare, likely functional variants within the general population62.

Somatic copy number alteration. Somatic copy number alterations (SCNAs) were identified in tumours with matched normal tissue using ASCAT (v3.1.2)63 in all autosomes and the chromosome X. The required hg38 reference files for processing WES data (loci, allele, GC correction and replication timing correction files) were downloaded from https://github.com/VanLoo-lab/ascat/tree/master/ReferenceFiles/WES (git commit ID 29f2fad). The loci and allele files were used as input to the ascat.perpareHTS function, along with tumour and matched normal BAM files. Other parameters used were as follows: genomeVersion=hg38, minCounts=10, min_base_qual=20, min_map_qual=35 and seed=485028101 for reproducibility. A BED file containing the genomic coordinates of the exome pull-down regions sequenced was also provided, as recommended. The sex parameter was determined by the clinical data provided for each patient, and alleleCount (v.4.3.0; https://github.com/cancerit/alleleCount) was also used. The outputs of ascat.prepareHTS were used to run the ascat.correctLogR function with the reference GC and replication timing files, and the ascat.aspcf function was then run with penalty = 70 and seed = 483024451 for reproducibility. Finally, the ascat.runAscat function was run using gamma=1 to estimate purity, ploidy and allele-specific copy number at each loci. Cases with a solution with a goodness-of-fit score <0.9 were considered noisy and excluded from further analysis.

To find significant recurrent amplifications and deletions, the outputs from ASCAT were used to generate input files for GISTIC2 (v2.0.23)64, which requires segment coordinates, the number of markers and a log2-scaled copy number. For each segment obtained from segmentation from ASCAT analysis, the normalised depth log ratio was extracted, and the number of assessed loci within each segment was used as the number of markers. GISTIC2 was run with the following parameters: -refgene hg38.UCSC.add_miR.160920.refgene.mat -gene-gistic 1 -smallmem 1 -broad 1 -brlen 0.75 -conf 0.95 -armpeel 1 -save-gene 1 -gcm extreme -v 20 -ta 0.25 -td 0.25. The hg38.UCSC.add_miR.160920.refgene.mat file is included with GISTIC2. The threshold for the residual q-value for both broad and focal amplifications and deletions was set at 0.10. To remove artefactual recurrent SCNAs, we further removed GISTIC2 wide peaks with an overlap of more than 40% with regions known to be problematic for sequencing and/or read mapping, as defined by the Genome in a Bottle Consortium benchmark union set of all difficult regions (v3.3; https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ReferenceSamples/giab/release/genome-stratifications/v3.3/GRCh38@all/Union/GRCh38_alldifficultregions.bed.gz). Finally, we also excluded a wide peak if the list of samples predicted to have a particular SCNA in GISTIC2 did not concur with the original ASCAT results.

Driver genes. To identify driver genes, we used dNdscv v0.1.0 (git commit ID 64f8443)65, which detects genes under positive selection in cancer. The reference gene annotations and covariates files used to run dNdScv were provided in the dNdScv package (RefCDS_human_GRCh38_GencodeV18_recommended.rda and covariates_hg19_hg38_epigenome_pcawg.rda, respectively). The outputs include p-values that were adjusted using the Benjamini & Hochberg method, and the q-value threshold was set at 0.10. A gene was selected if any of the q-values for substitutions and indels combined, substitutions only, missense mutations, nonsense mutations or indels only was below the q-value threshold. For patients with more than one tumour, variants were first merged to create a composite sample by patient prior to running dNdScv.

Hypothesising that the identification of several drivers might have been missed when testing all genes, restricted hypothesis testing (RHT) was performed considering 312 previously reported cancer driver genes17.

OnodriveFML (v2.4.0)66 was also used to identify candidate driver genes. OncodriveFML determines whether the average functional impact score of somatic mutations on an element (in this case, a coding gene) is significantly higher than expected, OncodriveFML was run with the following parameters: genome build, hg38; sequencing, wes; signature method, complement; classifier=CANCER_TYPE; statistic method, amean; sampling, 100,000; sampling max, 1,000,000; sampling chunk, 100; sampling minobs, 10; include indels, true; indel method, max; indel max consecutive, 7. Functional impact scores for the genome were downloaded from Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD; v1.7) website (https://cadd.gs.washington.edu; https://krishna.gs.washington.edu/download/CADD/v1.7/GRCh38/whole_genome_SNVs.tsv.gz). A regions file consisting of 100bp padded bait set regions was used. A gene was considered significantly mutated if it was mutated in at least 2 samples and had q<0.1.

Mutually exclusive and co-occurring interactions in driver genes (DISCOVER). DISCOVER20 was used to identify mutually exclusive and frequently co-occurring mutations. A binarised alteration matrix was generated for 17657 genes across the 197 primary STs with associated matched normal, where 0 and 1 indicated the absence or presence of a nonsynonymous mutation, respectively. Using the DISCOVER R package v.0.9.4, pairwise tests were performed for all genes which were altered in at least 10 STs. The tests were performed (i) with no stratification by ST subtype, (ii) with stratification by ST subtype, (iii) with stratification by MMR status and (iv) with stratification by ST subtype and MMR status. A false discovery rate (FDR) of 5% was applied to determine statistically significant mutual exclusivities and co-occurrences, focusing on the 28 driver genes called by dNdScv (Supplementary Data 6).

Mutational signatures. To identify somatic mutational signatures for single base substitutions, doublet base substitutions, and indels, somatic mutations from tumours with matched normal tissue were analysed using SigProfilerExtractor (v1.1.21)67. SigProfilerExtractor performs de novo extraction of mutational signatures and assigns known signatures to samples by refitting known COSMIC signatures to the extracted signatures using SigProfilerAssignment68. SigProfilerExtractor was run in exome mode using GRCh38 as the reference and opportunity genome, 500 replicates for non-negative matrix factorisation (NMF) with 1 to 10 signatures. The solution implemented for downstream analysis was the optimal solution provided by SigProfilerExtractor (referred to as the suggested solution). Results from signature decomposition and assignment were taken forward if the cosine similarity between the de novo extracted signatures and signatures reconstructed from assigned COSMIC signatures was ≥0.9. Similarly, on a per-sample basis, signature analysis was considered reliable if the cosine similarity between the original mutational spectrum and reconstructed spectrum was ≥0.9 and there were at least 100 mutations per sample, for each signature type (SBS, DBS, ID).

Germline variant calling. Reads aligned using BWA-MEM50 against the GRCh38 reference, and PCR duplicates were marked using Picard’s MarkDuplicates v2.25.4 (https://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/). Germline variants were identified from whole-exome data from normal samples using GATK v4.2.6.169 following GATK Best Practices70 for cohort calling of SNP and short INDELs. Variants were first called using GATK’s HaplotypeCaller in -ERC GVCF mode with parameters -G StandardAnnotation, -G StandardHCAnnotation, -G AS_StandardAnnotation. Followed by the creation of a genomicsdb database using GenomicsDBImport. Finally, joint genotyping was performed using GenotypeGVCFs. We separated SNP and INDELs using Picard’s SelectVariants v2.27.1. Subsequently, we used Picard’s VariantFiltration v2.27.1 to hard filter variants. For SNPs we filtered out variants: outside 100bp upstream or downstream from the baitset regions, QUAL< 30.0, SOR>3.0, FS>60, MQ<40, MQRankSum<−12.5 and ReadPosRankSum<−8.0. For indels, we filtered out variants: outside 100bp up and downstream from the baitset coordinates used, QD< 2.0, QUAL<30.0, FS>200.0 and ReadPosRankSum <−20.0. High-quality variants functional consequences were annotated using Ensembl Variant Effect Predictor (VEP) v103 using the same parameters, and additional annotations from ClinVar (Updated 2023.11), COSMIC, and gnomAD were added, as the somatic variants. Only indels ≤10bp were kept. To identify variants present within known germline cancer predisposition genes, we looked for variants present within the set of genes reported to be used by England’s National Health Service (NHS) Cancer National Genomic Test Directory v7.2 June 2023 [https://www.england.nhs.uk/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/Cancer-national-genomic-test-directory-version-7.2-June-2023.xlsx] to diagnose cancer predisposition in patients. Only variants with predicted moderate or High Impact over the encoded protein were reported. Variants found in POT1 were removed, as after manual inspection, they appeared to be artefactual.

Ancestry analysis. We projected the germline single-nucleotide polymorphisms from the whole-exome sequencing normal samples into the principal component space of the 1000 Genomes (1000G) project71 using the package AKT v0.3.372. Reported country of birth was aligned with projected super population by visual inspection of 1000G individuals alongside study individuals in the first four principal components, this confirmed that most individuals were either of European or East Asian ancestry.

MMR status. MMR status was defined based on 3 criteria, such as MMR expression (MLH1, MSH2, MSH6 and PMS2) by immunohistochemistry, indels rate and dMMR mutational signatures. Tumours were called dMMR when presenting loss of expression of at least one MMR, high indels rate (>10/Mb) and/or at least one dMMR signature (SBS and/or ID). In contrast, tumours were named pMMR when showing retained expression of MMR, low indels rate (<10/Mb) and/or no dMMR signatures (SBS and/or ID). Of note, tumours with no matched normal presented a higher mutational burden/indels rate due to the lack of accurate SNP filtering.

However, when statistically testing the best predictor for dMMR detection (i.e., indel rate versus tumour mutational burden; TMB (including SNVs, MNVs and indels), only confirmed dMMR and pMMR tumours were selected, in which IHC and somatic/germline variant calling where available. dMMR STs were retained when showing a MMR loss of expression, in addition to a biallelic mutation of an MMR genes.

Transcriptome
Fusion genes. Gene fusion identification was performed using STAR-Fusion v1.10.173, with STAR v2.78a and the Trinity Cancer Transcriptome Analysis Toolkit (CTAT) genome library StarFv1.10 for GRCh38 using GENCODE v37 (Ensembl v103) gene annotation. To assess the coding effect of the fusions and to annotate their presence in previous databases and validate them in silico, we used FusionInspector v2.6.0 by running STAR-Fusion with the parameters —FusionInspector validate —examine_coding_effect —denovo_reconstructFusion. Subsequently, we filtered out gene fusions: fusions with the total number of Junction read counts plus Spanning frag counts <5, FFPM<0.1, not a predicted coding effect, annotated as previously reported in normal tissues of the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project or neighbours. Collation of results, filtering, summaries per cohort and plotting was performed using custom scripts. Fusion gene structures were plotted using the Chimeraviz v1.24.074 package in R. In cases where data for multiple samples for the same patient was available, we used only a single sample to report the observed frequency of fused gene pairs within the cohorts.

Cell-fraction estimation of the tumour microenvironment (TME). The Immune Estimation module of TIMER2.0 (Tumour Immune Estimation Resource version 2)75 for immune infiltration estimation was run on the tumour samples. TPM-normalised, gene by sample, expression matrices were provided as input to the TIMER2.0 shiny web server (http://timer.cistrome.org/), selecting AUTO as the cancer type. Using EPIC output from TIMER2, cell-fraction estimation of nine cell types relevant to the TME of skin malignancies were obtained: B cells, cancer associated fibroblasts (CAFs), CD4+ T cells, CD8+ T cells, endothelial cells, tumour cells, and macrophages. These data were used alongside other data for the integrative clustering (described below).

Whole exome and transcriptome
Integrative clustering. Pre-processing of mutation data: SNVs and indels were collated per gene into a binary matrix, with 1s if the gene was mutated in a sample and 0 if the gene was wild-type. The selection of features was based on three criteria: first, genes which were at least mutated in 50 samples were selected. Second, those genes with mutations in at least 15 samples were tested (using a t-test) for association between the presence of mutation and total mutational burden in the tumour. Those genes with a p-value larger than 0.01 after FDR (false discovery rate) correction were selected, as those corresponded to genes where the presence of a mutation is not associated with high mutational burden in the tumour. Finally, based on biological knowledge, cancer genes such as TP53, MSH2, MSH6, MLH1, PMS2 were also included (if not selected by previous rules), and others like TTN, MUC6 and OBSCN were excluded (these genes are FLAGS76, i.e., these are genes often non-pathogenic and passengers, but are frequently mutated in most of the public exome studies). In total, 84 genes were selected.

Pre-processing of RNA-SEQ data: First, transcripts were mapped to gene symbols. In cases where more than one transcript corresponded to the same gene, the transcript with the higher interquartile range (IQR) was selected. Then, the RNA-SEQ read count matrix was converted to transcripts per million kilobases (TPMs) and log transformed (log(1+TPM)). In addition, the voom transformation77 was applied to attain a more suitable distribution for linear modelling. Next, the IQR of each gene was computed, and the 1000 genes that showed the most variability in expression were selected for clustering. We also added to this list the genes selected from the mutation list described above to account for cis-effects, ending up with 1082 genes. This number provided a good balance between high variance in the expression and a reasonable number of features for the computational performance of the Integrative Clustering algorithm. Finally, each gene was standardised to a z-score.

Sample selection: Only one sample replicate per tumour was chosen. Tumours with a diagnosis of SA, SM, SC-E and SC-O were selected, for a total of 170 tumours.

Integrative cluster algorithm. MOFA78 was used to fit a regularised latent variable model-based clustering. This model assumes a series of latent variables to represent k different molecular drivers that predict the observed combination of genomic and transcriptomic values in the tumours. These variables represent continuous activation levels of the different driver processes. The mutation data, represented with a binomial distribution and the expression data, represented with a Gaussian distribution, are connected to the latent driver processes via a parametric joint model. Regularisation is incorporated in the model to reduce model complexity and perform automatic feature selection.

We used the default number of factors (15), studied the robustness of the models fitting 10 runs and comparing the outputs, and selected the best model using the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO) criteria. We observed that only the first 10 factors explained at least 1% of the variability, and we decided to cluster the tumours based on those first 10 latent variables.

We performed hierarchical clustering using the Ward method on the Euclidean distance matrix and selected the best partition using the silhouette index criteria, composed of 9 clusters. We compared alternative solutions and found that this solution provided also the most meaningful structure.

To interpret the most common features of each group, we compared the frequency of mutations in each cluster and conducted differential expression between the tumours in that cluster and the rest using limma79. Finally, we conducted gene ontology enrichment analysis of those differentially expressed genes using the package clusterProfiler80, correcting the p-values with FDR and selecting those pathways enriched with an FDR <0.05, either over or under represented.

Neoantigen prediction. Class-I and -II haplotyping and neoantigen prediction were performed using the nextNEOpi nextflow pipeline81. Both DNA and RNA were used for predictions where available. Class-I and -II haplotypes for each sample were ascertained using Optitype82 and HLA-HD83, respectively. Variant calling was performed using Mutect284, Varscan285, Manta86 and Strelka287. Variants called by Mutect2 and at least one other caller were selected as candidate neoepitopes. Clonality of neoantigens were determined by ASCAT87 and Sequenza88. Further assessment of peptide-HLA binding was performed by pVACseq from the pVACtools suite89,90. Finally, neoantigenicity was evaluated by a Cauchy-Schwarz index of Neoantigens (CSiN)91.

Pathogen sequence analysis. Screening for pathogens used Kraken292 v2.1.2. Unfiltered paired-end whole exome and transcriptome sequencing FASTQ files were supplied as input, which was run with a 16GB-capped reference database containing RefSeq sequences from archaea, bacteria, viruses, plasmids, humans, UniVec_Core, protozoa, fungi, and plants [https://benlangmead.github.io/aws-indexes/k2] (version of March 2023). The following Kraken2 settings were used to generate i) report-style outputs: —paired —gzip-compressed —use-names —confidence 0.1 —db path/to/DB —report path/to/report —report-minimiser-data —output /dev/null path/to/fastq1 path/to/fastq2; ii) MPA-style outputs: kraken2 —paired —gzip-compressed —use-names —confidence 0.1 —db path/to/DB —report path/to/report —use-mpa-style —output /dev/null path/to/fastq1 path/to/fastq2. A confidence score threshold (—confidence) of 0.1 was applied to compensate the risk of false positives that is inherent to the method [https://github.com/DerrickWood/kraken2/blob/master/docs/MANUAL.markdown]. Using Kraken2 results, the proportion of minimisers was calculated from Kraken2’s reference database found in each sample for each taxon according to:

Proportion = (Number of distinct minimisers in input read data) / (Total clade level minimisers) (1)

To assess the significance of the results, a normal distribution was used to calculate the right-tailed probability of finding at least m minimisers, out of the total M minimisers available for a taxon, in n reads of a sample, considering the total N reads evaluated by Kraken2 in that sample. The Benjamini-Hochberg method93 was performed to correct for multiple comparisons. Results whose adjusted p-value was smaller than 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

Impact of alterations in pathway activations. Hippo and Yap1 pathway activations were computed based on the REACTOME definitions downloaded from the Molecular Signatures Database94 using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis with the R package gsva95. Next, we identified potential molecular aberrations that might have an effect on the inactivation of these pathways96. Each mutation was classified as follows: for oncogenes, missense variants, splice acceptor variants and splice donor variants were classified as activating mutations. For tumour suppressor genes, frameshift variants, start-lost, stop-gained and stop-lost variants were classified as truncating mutations. We also computed loss of heterozygosity using the copy number data. In order to test the association of the presence of these mutations with changes in the activation levels of the pathway, we performed a linear model and conducted a t-test on the parameters of the model.

MLH1 promoter hypermethylation testing. Analysis performed using tumour FFPE tissue derived DNA, which was bisulphite converted using the EpiTect Fast Bisulfit Kit. The methylation status of the tumour tissue was assessed by methylation sensitive high resolution melting analysis (MS-HRM), using MethylDetect MLH1 primer kits and EpiTech HRM PCR master mix on a Rotor-Gene Q 5Plex HRM platform. The MethylDetect MLH1 kit contains primers that amplify a region covering 5 CpG sites in the 5’ UTR region of the MLH1 gene (NM_000249.3), along with high-, low- and non-methylated control materials. MS-HRM data analysis was conducted using the Rotor-Gene Q Software v2.3.4 (build 3).

Ethics approval
Ethical approval was obtained from the different Institutes contributing to this project. Genetic analysis was further approved by the Sanger Human Materials and Data Management Committee.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This is a large and comprehensive study of genomic alterations in sebaceous neoplasms, reaching from benign to malignant tumors. The data generated represents a considerable resource, which is important for the scientific community. While the scope of the study and the number of samples is impressive, there are several significant weaknesses. Overall, it is not fully clear what novel aspects of these tumors has been revealed. The 5 mutational patterns are not fully convincing and the analysis of copy number changes and structural rearrangements not compelling as presented.
The manuscript is difficult to read with many nested sentences full of abbreviations and not always clear meaning and partially problematic grammar. More importantly, no coherent picture is distilled by integrating the multi-omic data to extend the knowledge on the biology of these tumors, i.e. what signaling pathways are consistently altered, what constitutes the barrier between benign and malignant, and how any of these features might relate to clinical course. Outcome data is mentioned to exist but does not seem to feature in the analysis.
Specific points:
1) Figure 1B y-axis labels should be clarified. What additional tumors qualify? Other STs. Could be phrased more clearly and succinctly.
2) Figure 1C is not referenced in the text and the labels are not clear. The pictures are clinical and histological and not clinicopathological
3) It would be good to show a lollipop diagram for RREB1 as well. Is there any information that can be gleaned about the functional relationship between RREB1 and HRAS mutations? For example, are particular types of RREB1 mutations associated with HRAS mutations? What are the anticipated functional consequences of RREB1 mutations?
4) The last sentence on mutually exclusivity is difficult to parse and the pattern of exclusivity not apparent (to me) from figure 2. It looks like many tumors with TP53 mutations also have mutations in RREB1, HRAS, or NOTCH1
5) The data on copy number changes implicating individual genes is not compelling. GISTIC scores in fig 5 looks noisy rather than showing bona fide copy number changes. This is particularly true for SA and SM, which seem to have overall ‘flat’ genomes. The sentence on page 8 line 342 onwards on amplifications of specific genes cannot be understood.
Also, what constitutes a ‘significantly focal amplification’? Compelling examples of the raw copy number data for example for HRNR and KIT amplifications should be shown for this section to be more compelling, ideally with additional supporting information nominating these genes (FISH, IHC). A better integration with mutation data is desirable when nominating specific genes based on copy number change. E.g. how would an amplification of GNAS be plausible in this tumor type, in which no activating mutations of GNAS are seemingly present?
The wording and grammar in these paragraphs is awkward e.g. ‘In contrast, SC-Es showed significantly chromosomes 1 and 20 amplifications, and significantly 17p deletions, which includes TP53 (7/36 tumours, of which 6 also had a somatic TP53 mutations’

### Reviewer 2

General comments:
In this multi-center international study, Ferreira et al. present the largest exome and transcriptome analysis of sebaceous tumors (ST) to date. This allowed investigators to identify mutated genes under positive selection (drivers) for the first time in this tumor type, which provides an incredibly valuable resource to the cancer research community. In my opinion, this is an extremely important study for the ST and cancer genomics fields.
The initial data processing, including variant calling, mutation signature extraction, and copy number profiling, was conducted using well-established software and pipelines. However, several downstream analyses are problematic, and the presentation of the results can be significantly improved to enhance clarity and better guide the reader. Furthermore, in my opinion, parts of the neoantigen and ligand-receptor analyses are too speculative, and they lack additional data or experimentation for validation. These sections should be modified for clarity and rigor, and their results presented more cautiously or the authors may want to consider omitting these analyses from the study.
My recommendation is to improve the whole exome and transcriptome analysis as outlined in detailed below and re- consider inclusion of the ligand-receptor analysis and parts of the neoantigen analysis.
Concerns/suggested revisions:
Somatic landscape of sebaceous tumours
Driver Identification Analysis:
[1] The paper reports significantly mutated genes based on a single software tool (dNdScv), without the necessary validation steps (e.g. filtering for genes that are not expressed or have low VAF), raising concerns about false positives that are ubiquitous in the context of high TMB tumors. (For example, SPANXB1 is reported as a driver in Figure 2, but most mutations in this gene appear to have a suspiciously low VAF). To ensure robustness, the authors should filter their results to exclude likely false positives and, importantly, provide additional supporting evidence for the novel candidate drivers:
● What is the variant allele frequency (VAF) distribution for each gene?
● Do these variants mostly originate from a specific signature or positional site?
● What proportion of variants are seen in the RNA-Seq data for each gene?
● Are there significant co-occurrences of loss-of-function mutations with loss of heterozygosity (LOH) for the putative tumor suppressor genes (TSGs)?
[1.1] The authors of the dNdScv software have excluded hypermutator samples (>500 mutations) from their main analysis (iMartincorena et al, 2017, PMID:29056346). Such precautions are not mentioned in the method section of the current manuscript. Did they authors try running dNdScv exclusively on tumors with fewer than, say, 1000 or 2000 mutations to see how it affects the results?
[1.2] There are 24 samples with no matched normal. It is important to exclude these samples from the dNdScv analysis as they could contain germline variants misclassified as somatic (I’ve noticed VAF modes near 0.5 for many of these samples). Could the authors specify which samples have been included in their analyses, along with any exclusion criteria?
[1.3] Possible additional figures for the driver analysis (in main or supplementary): A barplot showing the relative proportion of each variant class (missense, frameshift stop gain etc) in each gene or selected genes. A scatter plot showing dN/dS:missense vs dN/dS:Lof similar to Figure 2B in Martincorena et al.(2017, PMID: 29056346). These figures would help support the analysis results and importantly inform about the action mode of the candidate drivers (i.e. oncogene vs.TSG).
[1.4] It would be helpful if the authors cross-reference their gene list with the results of some pan-cancer analyses, such as Bailey et al. (2018, PMID: 29625053) or Martincorena et al. (2017, PMID: 29056346). This information could be easily summarized in a supplementary figure having genes as rows and cancer types as columns, with each tile colored according to their report status (e.g. oncogene, potential oncogene, tsg and potential tsg, which is available in Supplementary Table 1 of Bailey et al.). It would be useful for the readers for genes that haven’t been reported as significantly mutated, what does the literature say about them that could support their role as an oncogene or tumor suppressor?
[1.5] I speculate the authors may have missed the identification of several drivers by testing all genes as they did impose a burden on significance levels after multiple testing corrections. In addition to their global analysis, I think it may be worth performing a restricted hypothesis testing (RHT), such as in Lawrence et al. (2014, PMID: 24390350) by considering only previously reported genes, for example those from Bailey et al. (2018), and those reported as drivers in sebaceous tumors. This additional analysis would be straightforward, requiring only the subsetting of the global results to these genes before applying multiple testing corrections. This may be valuable to the readers.
[1.6] The main oncoplot could be enhanced in several ways.
• Adding copy number track for the most frequently affected genes (deleted TSG or amplified oncogenes).
• Some drivers with less supporting evidence or of lower interest could be removed from the main figure for simplicity and clarity (but shown in a full supplementary oncoplot).
• Annotation tracks with tumor purity, RNA subtypes and mutational signature groups could be added.
• Mode of action of each driver (TSG vs oncogene) could be highlighted.
[1.7] The authors only report the gene names with their corrected p-values in the supplementary material. It is important to include the complete dNdScv output in the supplementary material to provide a comprehensive view of the analysis and facilitate further validation and reproducibility of results.
[1.8] On lines 199-200, the authors write, "Interestingly, when considering the ST subtypes individually, HRAS was only identified as a driver gene in the benign tumors." What is the uncorrected p-value for HRAS in the SC-E and SC-O subgroup analyses? Would it pass RHT? Even if not significant, the oncoplot shows several HRAS mutations in SC-E and SC-O, most of which are known activating mutations at G12/13 and Q61. Moreover, HRAS harbors no silent mutations in these tumors, strongly suggesting it is an actual driver, albeit less frequently mutated. Accordingly, it would be more appropriate to drop this statement or at least revise it to "HRAS was not reported as significant in (...) probably due to its lower mutation frequency and the smaller size of these groups (...)," and mention the presence of these hotspot mutations. In general, the absence of a significant result for a particular gene in a subgroup analysis cannot be used on its own to suggest an absence of “driver” activity.
[1.9] In the discussion, lines 491-492, the authors state: “Use of somatic mutational profiling may help in the differential diagnosis of benign versus malignant STs, which can be challenging.” It would be helpful if more clinical context could be provided here, particularly around the standard histopathological diagnostic workflow. What are the gold-standard IHC stains, histopathological correlates, or clinical decision algorithms currently used to differentiate between the four types of sebaceous tumors? A deeper discussion on how mutational testing could provide clinical input would be ideal, given the clinical correlation angle in the discussion. Figure 2 does not clearly identify a mutational profile with high sensitivity or specificity for diagnosis. Could the authors consider using classifiers (e.g., Random Forests) and measure their performance with cross-validation?
Mutually exclusive and co-occurring mutations:
[2] The “mutual exclusions and co-occurring interactions” analysis is problematic as it combines the results of a Fisher’s test with the output of DISCOVER, a tool specifically developed to replace the inappropriate usage of the Fisher’s test in such analyses. The Fisher’s test does not control for TMB, leading to a high number of false positive co-occurring interactions (as shown in Figure 2B). In contrast, DISCOVER accounts for TMB in each sample and gene, thus limiting these spurious results. Combining the results from both approaches does not make sense, as exemplified by the contradictions between the interactions reported in Figure 2B and the DISCOVER analysis output provided in Supplementary Table 6 (e.g., significant co-occurrence between ZNF750 and BICRA while Supplementary Table 6 reports significant mutual exclusion). I would suggest that the authors should rely solely on DISCOVER (or similar approaches controlling for TMB), and completely exclude the Fisher’s test from this analysis.
Mutational signatures of sebaceous tumours:
[3] The mutational signature analysis was not comprehensively explored and presented, and a global view of the cohort is lacking, specifically related to the relative contribution of the main signatures in each sample. The presentation of the results in Figure S5 show too many signatures simultaneously, and additional figures and analyses would be necessary to support the claims and observations made in the main text and discussion. In my opinion, an improved global view of the mutational signatures would warrant inclusion as a main figure.
[3.1] Figure S5 needs clarification. The graphical legend mentions */PD A, */PD NA, and */PD NV in three different colors, but none of these are explained in the textual legend. There is a reference to the blue and red labeling of the sample names, but this is confusing since "blue" samples (no significant signature) actually show some signatures. Additionally, the legend states that "one in red text was not included," but half of the samples are in red.
[3.2] The method section states that SigProfilerExtractor was used for de novo extraction, considering solutions with 1 to 10 signatures by NMF. However, Supplementary Figure 5 shows 21 signatures (17 SBS, 3 ID, and 1 DBS), and Supplementary Table 8 reports mutation counts for 27 signatures. This discrepancy needs clarification. It is essential to explain the criteria for determining the final set of signatures and how they relate to the initial NMF analysis to ensure consistency and transparency.
[3.3] I strongly suggest the authors include a main figure summarizing the mutational signature analysis. For example, a clustered heatmap of each signature log10 counts (as rows) in each sample (columns) clearly shows the 3 main mutational profiles within this cohort: MMR (SBS15 + ID2 + ID7 + high SBS1 + high SBS5), UV (DBS1 + SBS7a + SBS7b + low SBS1 + low SBS5) and others (low SBS1 + low SBS5). Annotation tracks for samples could include the MMR status, log10TMB, diagnosis and presence/absence of LoF mutations in MSH2 & MSH6. An annotation track for the signatures could inform the reader about their aetiology (UV, MMR etc). Such heatmap can be easily produced with R’s pheatmap package and the ward.D2 clustering method. To make it more concise and suitable for a main figure, some highly correlated or same aetiology signatures could be merged (e.g. SBS7a & SBS7b) and low contributing signatures could be dropped and deferred to supplementary figures (if necessary). Alternatively, the authors could use the W matrix from NMF or apply PCA on the 96-SBS mutation proportion matrix to create a scatter plot of all samples colored by cancer types, MMR status and other variables of interest.
[3.4] Lines 268-269, the authors write, “As expected, in the dMMR cases, the high TMB was attributed to dMMR-associated mutational signatures.” What proportion of TMB is attributed to dMMR signatures? Could the authors please include a figure supporting this? It seems that other signatures (SBS1 & SBS5) contribute more to TMB than dMMR-associated signatures, even in dMMR samples.
[3.5] Lines 163-166, the authors write, “Interestingly, indel rate rather than TMB, more accurately predicted MMR status (indel rate p-value < 2.2e-16 versus TMB rate p-value = 2.203e-08, Welch two samples t-test)”. I have a few concerns regarding this analysis. First, the considered data doesn’t meet this test's assumptions about normality. Second, p-values are not an appropriate measure of prediction accuracy. Third, according to the methods section, MMR status was in part determined by the indel rate (lines 772-774), which means using the indel rate to predict MMR status is circular reasoning. These issues should be addressed, for example by comparing ROC-AUCs and and an MMR classification that doesn’t rely on indel rate or TMB.
[3.6] On lines 501-513, the authors write “this study highlights the importance of recording the precise location of SC-O tumours, and specifically restricting use of the term SC-O for only those arising on the eyelid. Indeed, the sample coming from the canthus showed a different phenotype from the other SC-O, being characterised by UV mutational signatures rather than being pauci-mutated”. Could the authors please include a figure and additional analyses or references supporting this claim, for example by showing differences in mutated drivers or gene expression that suggest it is more similar to SC-E than SC-O?
[3.7] Lines 1377-1379: “SBS” should be “DBS”. Also, a typo in “mutationa”.
[3.8] In some other cancers, MMR status is linked to survival (e.g. Endometrial). Did the authors investigate whether in this cohort, MMR status is linked to survival in SC regardless of subtype? Authors note that sample size in SC was too small to measure but it may be helpful for readers to see this information anyways even if not statistically significant.
Integrative cluster analysis:
[4] The results of this analysis are rather cryptic, and the methodological details raise concerns about their validity. First, the expression data was combined with the mutation profiles of approximately 80 genes selected on the basis that they are frequently mutated in this cohort. Given that a typical tumor contains fewer than 10-15 driver mutations (referring here to Martincorena et al, 2017) and that these sebaceous tumors have huge TMBs (nearly half of them have a thousand mutations or more), we can be sure that most of the mutations in these 80 genes are passenger mutations. While a few relevant genes such as TP53 and MSH2 have been manually added and others like TTN have been manually removed, Supplementary Figure 4 suggests that the limited number of potentially meaningful mutations is still overwhelmed by the number of passengers.
Second, the method contains many steps with somehow arbitrary choices (e.g., a first selection step out of 16 fitted models followed by a second selection step for the number of k-means clusters), making it very difficult to assess the robustness of the findings. What happens if we use another fitted model (many had a similar balance of variance explained and a low number of clusters)? What happens if a different k is chosen or if we change the gene sets?
I should note, even if the authors are able to address the concerns described above, and although I appreciate these exploratory types of integrative analysis, I would argue they cannot replace the more well-established analyses that many readers would expect, if only for clarity and easier interpretation of the results. In other words:
[4.1] How many (purely) transcriptional groups seem to be there? If the exact number is hard to determine, the smallest number that make sense (visually) should be the starting point.
[4.2] Once these groups have been identified, do they correspond to the ST subtypes (SA vs. SC-E vs. SC-O)?
[4.3] Are they enriched for specific mutations or CNAs?
[4.4] Which immune and other non -tumor cell types are present in each of these bulk tumors? How does this correlate with tumor purity?
[4.5] Which pathways or genes seems differentially expressed between these groups? Could this be confounded by tumor purity or non-tumor cells or is there evidence that they could represent genuine differences between the cancerous or neoplastic cells?

## Authors' Response to Round 1

We thank Reviewer1 for their constructive comments and insights. As mentioned, we have collected the largest ever dataset of sebaceous tumours, comparing benign (sebaceous adenoma and sebaceoma) and malignant (extra-ocular and peri-ocular sebaceous carcinoma) cohorts which we have examined through extensive computational analyses.
We were able to identify several novel aspects in this study:
1. We discovered (and validate statistically) new driver genes (for example HRAS, MSH2/MLH1, RB1) not previously reported in sebaceous tumours and profiled the full spectrum of mechanisms by which previously reported genes are altered to become drivers (i.e. somatic mutation and/or somatic copy number alterations (deletion, amplification or cnLOH)). For example, we detected copy neutral LOH of mismatch repair (MMR) genes and amplification of other drivers such as GNAS, PLAG1 and Hornerin. We also describe new fusions and importantly show that PAK fusions are not restricted to apocrine poromas – this is of clinical/diagnostic significance. Remarkably, we also identified pathogenic (exonuclease proofreading defects) POLE/POLD1 somatic mutations, not previously reported to be linked to sebaceous tumours.
2. We also show, for the first time, that tumours may take different paths to tumourigenesis. For example, Lynch patients can carry STs with a germline and somatic mutations, as well as a germline mutation and a cnLOH event. While other tumours which are pMMR, specifically SCs, exhibited biallelic inactivation of TP53 co-occuring with ZNF750 and/or RB1 disruption (particularly SC-O), suggesting TP53 might accelerate ZNF750/RB1-driven SC as occurs for BRAF p.V600E in melanoma. In support of this hypothesis, concomitant TP53/RB1 mutations were identified in some metastatic SC cases. This study reinforces the important role of RB1 in malignant STs, with inactivation occurring via somatic mutation, focal deletion (in SC-E) and 13q deletion (in SC-O). Moreover, the spectrum of the somatic mutations in the tumours across the same individual can vary (see patient PD43887).
3. We clearly found that sebaceous tumours have a propensity to develop in the context of a high mutational burden including mismatch repair (MMR) deficiency and UV-damage as previously reported, but also POLE/POLD1 somatic mutation and APOBEC activation. In addition, MLH1 promoter hypermethylation was revealed as a rare event in sebaceous tumours, associated with somatic dMMR.
4. We also show that clinical variables such as developing a sebaceous tumour outside the head and neck area, having multiple sebaceous tumours, and presenting with another non-sebaceous Lynch syndrome related neoplasm are good Lynch syndrome predictors. In addition, histopathological variables such as no epidermal connection, tumour delimitated by a collarette, KA-like architecture and diagnosis of SM are also good LS predictors, with clinical variables being better predictors.
5. We demonstrated that indel rate is more reliable than TMB in defining dMMR. In skin, UV-damage increases the TMB and the level of these mutations differs depending on the site and age of the patient, while a high indel burden is largely acquired as a result of dMMR.
6. The method applied to detect Lynch syndrome via the analysis of colon tumours cannot be directly applied to sebaceous tumours. Indeed, unlike colorectal cancers, somatic BRAF p.V600E and MLH1 promoter hypermethylation testing is not relevant to STs and cannot be employed to distinguish sporadic from germline dMMR tumours owing to the absence of BRAF p.V600E mutations in these tumours and our observation that hypermethylation of the MLH1 promoter is a rare event in sporadic dMMR STs.
7. The use of somatic mutational profiling may help in the differential diagnosis of benign versus malignant STs, which can be challenging. For example, malignant STs were driven by chromosomal instability and typically showed biallelic TP53 inactivation, as well as TP53 mutations co-occurring with ZNF750 and/or RB1 mutations. In addition, dMMR SC-E was characterised by mutations in NOTCH1, RREB1, and DRD5, whereas SC-O was characterised by significant focal amplifications encompassing GNAS/SALL4 and LYN/PLAG1, significant broad 13q deletions (encompassing BRCA2 and RB1), and 8q amplifications (encompassing MYC), with amplification of the MYC proto-oncogene previously reported by targeted sequencing and FISH11. Lastly, both SC-E and SC-O showed significant amplification of chromosomes 1q21.3 and 20. The former amplification encompasses HNRN (Hornerin), which is part of the epidermal differentiation complex on 1q21. Hornerin is expressed by the ocular surface (corneal and conjunctival aspects, including meibomian and Zeis glands), the lacrimal apparatus and the skin, and has antimicrobial and protective (keratinisation) functions 47,48, reinforcing its potential role in sebaceous carcinoma. STs, with the exception of SC-O, can be the first sentinel sign of LS and 3 clinical criteria and 4 histopathological criteria – including (i) the presence of multiple STs, (ii) STs being located outside the head and neck area, (iii) the presence of a LS-associated cancer, in the clinical model, and (i) the absence of epidermal connection, (ii) the delimitation of the ST by a collarette, (iii) a KA-like architecture, and (iv) the diagnosis of SM in the histopathological model, together with loss of MMR expression by IHC – were found to significantly associate with a LS diagnosis (the clinical model being a better predictor) and thus should raise the index of suspicion that could provoke a referral for germline genetic testing. Of note, while the idea of generating a classifier is one we feel is very validate, a comparable dataset of STs to the one we describe in our paper does not exist which makes validating such a tool problematic and thus we feel this analysis is premature. Further, this study highlights the importance of recording the precise location of SC-O tumours, and specifically restricting use of the term SC-O to those lesions arising on the eyelid. Indeed, the sample coming from the canthus showed a different phenotype from the other SC-O and was characterised by a UV mutational signature, rather than being pauci-mutated, the pattern observed in SC-Os.
Despite the enormous size of this cohort and the deep characterization we are still not powered enough to make conclusions about patient outcome because at the time of writing only 4 patients had died of their disease.
Addressing specifically the point about multi-omic/data integration – in Figure 3 we integrate our SNV and expression catalogue to define 9 statistically significant groups.
Regarding the grammar, we have reviewed this carefully and had a professional editor review the text prior to resubmission.

Tile plots do not consider gene length or sequence context or variant consequence, which is considered in the statistical model deployed within DISCOVER meaning that it can be difficult to decern genetic interactions by looking at these profiles alone. We note that our analysis with DISCOVER (and also with Fishers; removed from the revised manuscript as requested by the reviewers) was performed without stratification for tumour type, thus including the SC-O cases where the mutual exclusivity between the abovementioned genes is more evident.
We have reviewed these associations and they remain statistically robust.
TP53 and HRAS were statistically mutually exclusive, which was demonstrated by DISCOVER (adjusted pvalue = 0.00091) and Fisher (one-tailed pvalue = 0.0381) tests. Although we have samples with both mutations, it was defined as statistically significant, likely driven by SC-O.
We also ran DIALECT (Shuaibi A et al. 2024; https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11071465/), an alternative algorithm for identifying co-occurring and mutually exclusive interactions. We have changed significantly focal to significant focal amplification.
To find significant recurrent amplifications and deletions, the output of ASCAT was used to generate input files for GISTIC2 (v2.0.23)65, which requires segment coordinates, the number of markers and a log2-scaled copy number for each segment. GISTIC2 was run with the following parameters: -refgene hg38.UCSC.add_miR.160920.refgene.mat -genegistic 1 -smallmem 1 -broad 1 -brlen 0.75 -conf 0.95 -armpeel 1 -savegene 1 -gcm extreme -v 20 -ta 0.25 -td 0.25. The hg38.UCSC.add_miR.160920.refgene.mat file is included with GISTIC2.
The threshold for the residual q-value for both broad and focal amplifications and deletions was set at 0.10. To identify driver events, we focused on genes within significant amplifications and deletions <= 10Mb in size. To remove artefactual recurrent SCNAs, we further removed GISTIC2 wide peaks with an overlap of more than 40% with regions known to be problematic for sequencing and/or read mapping, as defined by the Genome in a Bottle Consortium benchmark union (v3.3; https://ftp-trace.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/ReferenceSamples/giab/release/genome-stratifications/v3.3/GRCh38@all/Union/GRCh38_alldifficultregions.bed.gz). Finally, we also excluded a wide peak if the list of samples predicted to have a particular SCNA in GISTIC2 did not concur with the original ASCAT results.
i.e. to be defined as a significant focal copy number event a region needs to have a GISTIC2 residual q-value < 0.1, a peak size > 100,000bp, show concordance with the ASCAT CN call of >= 0.75, and for the region to not overlap with a Genome In A Bottle "difficult regions" by >40%.

Several cancer-related genes are frequently amplified but not commonly mutated in tumours. Amplification generally refers to the increase in the number of copies of a particular gene, which can lead to overexpression/mis-expression of the encoded protein and in this way contribute to tumorigenesis. This does not have to be with concomitant mutation of the gene.
Here are some key examples:
1. ERBB2 (HER2/neu)
- Function: Encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cell growth and differentiation.
- Amplification: Commonly amplified in breast cancer, gastric cancer, and other solid tumours.
- Clinical Significance: Overexpression of HER2 is associated with aggressive tumour behaviour and poor prognosis. HER2-targeted therapies (e.g., trastuzumab) are effective in treating cancers with HER2 amplification.
2. MYC (c-MYC)
- Function: Encodes a transcription factor that regulates genes involved in cell proliferation, growth, and metabolism.
- Amplification: Often amplified in various cancers, including breast cancer, lung cancer, and neuroblastoma.
- Clinical Significance: MYC amplification is associated with high tumour grade, aggressive behaviour, and poor prognosis.
3. MDM2
- Function: Encodes a protein that inhibits the tumour suppressor p53.
- Amplification: Frequently amplified in sarcomas, glioblastomas, and certain carcinomas.
- Clinical Significance: MDM2 amplification leads to p53 inactivation, contributing to tumour progression. It is a potential target for cancer therapies.
4. CCND1 (Cyclin D1)
- Function: Encodes a protein that regulates cell cycle progression.
- Amplification: Commonly amplified in breast cancer, head and neck cancers, and lymphomas.
- Clinical Significance: Cyclin D1 overexpression due to gene amplification drives cell proliferation, making it a target for therapeutic intervention.
5. EGFR (Epidermal Growth Factor Receptor)
- Function: Encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cell growth and survival.
- Amplification: Frequently amplified in glioblastomas, non-small cell lung cancer, and other tumours.
- Clinical Significance: EGFR amplification is associated with increased cell proliferation and survival, and EGFR-targeted therapies are used in treating certain cancers.
6. MET
- Function: Encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cellular growth, motility, and survival.
- Amplification: Often amplified in gastric cancer, lung cancer, and papillary renal cell carcinoma.
- Clinical Significance: MET amplification can lead to constitutive activation of the receptor, driving oncogenesis. Targeted therapies against MET are being developed.
7. CDK4
- Function: Encodes a cyclin-dependent kinase that plays a key role in cell cycle progression.
- Amplification: Commonly amplified in melanoma, sarcoma, and glioblastoma.
- Clinical Significance: CDK4 amplification promotes cell cycle progression and is a target for CDK4/6 inhibitors in cancer therapy.
8. FGFR1 (Fibroblast Growth Factor Receptor 1)
- Function: Encodes a receptor tyrosine kinase involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, and angiogenesis.
- Amplification: Amplified in lung squamous cell carcinoma, breast cancer, and other tumours.
- Clinical Significance: FGFR1 amplification drives tumorigenesis, and FGFR inhibitors are being explored in clinical trials.
These genes are frequently amplified in various cancers, only occasionally with mutation, and their amplification often plays a critical role in driving tumour progression, making them key targets for cancer therapies.

Out of the two sebaceomas samples from this patient sample PD43859a did not passed DNA QC. Thus, to explore the question of a shared clonal origin further we compared the mutations found in the DNA/exome sequence of PD43859c to variants called from the transcriptome sequence of PD43859a.
This analysis revealed:
 Of the 7 sites called as somatic variants from PD43859c with sufficient coverage in PR43859a 5 / 7 variant calls were concordant. i.e. they appear as somatic variants in both PR43859a and PD43859c.
 If we consider all sites, at least 8 / 15 ((5+3) / 15) variants in ‘c’ are found in ‘a’; however, 5 sites had coverage < 10X and therefore may be false negatives.
Collectively, these observations do suggest a shared origin for a and c. However, these two samples were both benign and collected with a time gap of 3 years between each excision. This time gap means that it is unlikely to be a recurrence. We therefore wonder if these tumours have a shared, possibly post-zygotic, origin with this specific patient noted as having multiple (many) sebaceous cysts in their clinical notes. This is an intriguing observation indeed.
8) The finding on CIN primarily in pMMR tumors is interesting and mirrors the findings in CRC. This indicates, as you state, that genomic instability is necessary for the malignant transformation. Any insights on why and how?
Comparisons of CIN (measured in terms of numbers of gains and losses of chromosome arms or long DNA segments therein) in pMMR and dMMR colorectal cancers (CRC) has shown a clear difference with pMMR CRCs showing significantly more CIN than dMMR CRCs. These data are consistent with the hypothesis that at least one form of genomic instability, either CIN as seen in the majority of CRC that are pMMR, or dMMR is required to allow transformation to malignancy. Here, we hypothesise similar mechanisms occurring in sebaceous tumours with CIN in pMMR or MSI in dMMR cases. Underlying CIN there can be increased replication stress and defects in mitotic spindle assembly, errors in chromosome cohesion and segregation, centrosome amplification, and/or dysfunctional checkpoints. Telomere dysfunction and epigenetic mechanisms may also contribute.

In this multi-center international study, Ferreira et al. present the largest exome and transcriptome analysis of sebaceous tumors (ST) to date. This allowed investigators to identify mutated genes under positive selection (drivers) for the first time in this tumor type, which provides an incredibly valuable resource to the cancer research community. In my opinion, this is an extremely important study for the ST and cancer genomics fields.

The initial data processing, including variant calling, mutation signature extraction, and copy number profiling, was conducted using well-established software and pipelines. STs, with the exception of SC-O, can be the first sentinel sign of LS and 3 clinical criteria and 4 histopathological criteria – including (i) the presence of multiple STs, (ii) STs being located outside the head and neck area, (iii) the presence of a LS-associated cancer, in the clinical model, and (i) the absence of epidermal connection, (ii) the delimitation of the ST by a collarette, (iii) a KA-like architecture, and (iv) the diagnosis of SM in the histopathological model, together with loss of MMR expression by IHC – were found to significantly associate with a LS diagnosis (the clinical model being a better predictor) and thus should raise the index of suspicion that could provoke a referral for germline genetic testing. Of note, while the idea of generating a classifier is one we feel is very validate, a comparable dataset of STs to the one we describe in our paper does not exist which makes validating such a tool problematic and thus we feel this analysis is premature. Further, this study highlights the importance of recording the precise location of SC-O tumours, and specifically restricting use of the term SC-O to those lesions arising on the eyelid. Indeed, the sample coming from the canthus showed a different phenotype from the other SC-O and was characterised by a UV mutational signature, rather than being pauci-mutated, the pattern observed in SC-Os.”
Mutually exclusive and co-occurring mutations:
[2] The “mutual exclusions and co-occurring interactions” analysis is problematic as it combines the results of a Fisher’s test with the output of DISCOVER, a tool specifically developed to replace the inappropriate usage of the Fisher’s test in such analyses. The Fisher’s test does not control for TMB, leading to a high number of false positive co-occurring interactions (as shown in Figure 2B). In contrast, DISCOVER accounts for TMB in each sample and gene, thus limiting these spurious results. Combining the results from both approaches does not make sense, as exemplified by the contradictions between the interactions reported in Figure 2B and the DISCOVER analysis output provided in Supplementary Table 6 (e.g., significant co-occurrence between ZNF750 and BICRA while Supplementary Table 6 reports significant mutual exclusion). I would suggest that the authors should rely solely on DISCOVER (or similar approaches controlling for TMB), and completely exclude the Fisher’s test from this analysis.

The DIALECT software distinguishes between missense and nonsense mutation by design and claims to be superior to DISCOVER. However, even after talking to the authors and re-writing some of their code we were unable to deploy this algorithm.

Integrative cluster analysis:
[4] The results of this analysis are rather cryptic, and the methodological details raise concerns about their validity.
We agree that the integrative analysis was not properly described in the manuscript. In particular, we focused only on the clustering of tumours instead of the identification of molecular drivers, which is the main goal of this type of methods. We have now run two different methods: iCluster (https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btp543) and MOFA (https://doi.org/10.15252/msb.20178124), both of them based on latent variable analysis and performed a comprehensive study on the robustness of the results. In the end, we decided to use MOFA, as the fitting process is more robust, and the results were easier to interpret. We must note that the goal of this method is not clustering, but identification of molecular drivers. We have included these data in the revised manuscript along with text and figures to explain the results.
First, the expression data was combined with the mutation profiles of approximately 80 genes selected on the basis that they are frequently mutated in this cohort. Given that a typical tumor contains fewer than 10-15 driver mutations (referring here to Martincorena et al, 2017) and that these sebaceous tumors have huge TMBs (nearly half of them have a thousand mutations or more), we can be sure that most of the mutations in these 80 genes are passenger mutations. While a few relevant genes such as TP53 and MSH2 have been manually added and others like TTN have been manually removed, Supplementary Figure 4 suggests that the limited number of potentially meaningful mutations is still overwhelmed by the number of passengers.
The reviewer raises some interesting points. Indeed, the main goal of our integrative clustering is not so much to group tumours but to identify molecular driver events. To do that, both iCluster and MOFA methods identify sets of mutations and expression changes that co-occur in subsets of tumours. As both methods are computationally demanding, our first step in this analysis was feature selection. In the case of mutations, the reviewer is right that some of these tumours have a high mutational burden. We tried to identify a relatively small subset of genes that were potentially interesting, setting up filters based on the minimum number of samples that carry mutations. As the reviewer states, some of these could be passengers. We have added an additional filter testing for association of the mutation and the total mutational burden, removing those that were statistically significant. With this filter, we expected to remove those genes that were probably passengers. We also added manually some well-known driver genes. Of course, our final set of 84 genes might still contain some passenger genes, but both iCluster and MOFA will select only those that contribute to any driver event, as they contain regularisation to perform variable selection, removing uninteresting genes. In the case of expression, we used the 1,000 most expressed genes plus the genes present in the selected mutations.
Second, the method contains many steps with somehow arbitrary choices (e.g., a first selection step out of 16 fitted models followed by a second selection step for the number of k-means clusters), making it very difficult to assess the robustness of the findings. What happens if we use another fitted model (many had a similar balance of variance explained and a low number of clusters)? What happens if a different k is chosen or if we change the gene sets?
The optimal selection of the number of components is a well-known problem in Latent Variable Modelling and Cluster Analysis, and although several methods have been proposed, they often do not agree on the best solution. Starting with the selection of latent dimensions (that is, molecular drivers), MOFA is quite robust and in fact it recommends using the default number of 15. We checked the robustness of the models comparing the total variance explained and the minimum variance explained by any of the factors when we fitted a different number of latent factors in the model. As the plots below show, after 15 factors the increase in variance is minimal, therefore we used that value.
We also inspected the robustness in the model fitting using the recommended procedure in the vignette. We fitted our MOFA model using different random seeds and checked how similar the results were comparing the correlation of the factors obtained in each fit. We finally selected the best model.
It is also easy to quantify how much variance from each data type the latent factors explain, in order to focus on the most interesting drivers:
If we set up a threshold of minimum variance at 1%, we can retain for further study the first 10 latent factors. Indeed, they are the ones that contribute most to the tumours.
These drivers are characterised by both mutations:
And gene expression:
These plots show the weights of each feature in each latent factor. The larger (or smaller) the x-value (weight), the more important the feature is in defining that latent factor. For example, having mutations in TP53 or ZNF750 will produce a high score in Factor 3. Looking at those weights we can also see that Factor 1 is explained mostly by mutations, and not that much by expression. In fact, that factor explains 23.8% of the mutation data and only 0.54% of the expression. It reflects high mutational burden, as all mutations have a similar positive score.
The following heatmap shows the weights of each molecular driver (latent factor, columns) in each tumour (rows):
As we can see each tumour presents a combination of these drivers, therefore it makes sense to try to cluster tumours based on their score. Using the top 10 factors we identified two potential solutions with 7 or 9 subgroups based on the silhouette index. These solutions were almost identical; the two new clusters were partition of the first and the third cluster. The following heatmap allows us to compare and choose the best partition. In fact, 9 clusters seem to identify better the subgroup of tumours that have high scores in the first factor (high mutational burden) and splits the third cluster into a group with high scores of factor number 4. We kept the solution with 9 integrative subgroups.
We describe now the 9 molecular subgroups:
For each integrative cluster (IntClust 1 to 9), the following data will be available:
1) (n= ): the number of samples included into this IntClust;
2) Subtype: which tumour subtype is mostly included into the IntClust;
3) MMR: which MMR status represents the most the IntClust;
4) Indel and SNV rate: which compare the mentioned IntClust against all the others;
5) Proportion of cells: which compare the same cell type across the different Cluster and not the comparison between different cell type in a same Cluster;
6) Proportion of mutated tumours: which proportion of samples in this IntClust are mutated for a specific gene;
7) Pathway activation: activity of specific pathway in this IntClust;
8) Copy number aberration: CNA profile of the IntClust.
9) Mainly SC-O tumours.
IntClust 1(n=13 tumours):
A mutational-burden driven subgroup, mostly SM tumours with MMR deficiency and up-regulation of G2M checkpoint and E2F targets. High proportion of CD8+ T cells and fibroblasts.
IntClust 2(n=15 tumours):
Indel-driven cluster, but with lower indel levels. Mostly SM tumours. dMMR, MYC up-regulated and down-regulation in interferon response. High proportion of CD8+ T cells.
IntClust 3(n=13 tumours):
High indel burden, NOTCH1 and RREB1 mutations, dMMR but down-regulation of most hallmark pathways. High proportion of CD4+ T cells.
IntClust 4(n=23 tumours):
Lower mutational burden, but large proportion of TP53 mutations. Many copy number aberrations and upregulation of interferon response. pMMR. High immune population (B cells and T cells in particular)
IntClust 5(n=34 tumours):
Mostly SA tumours with high mutational burden. Few copy number aberrations and many up-regulated pathways though. High B cells proportion.
IntClust 6 (n=20 tumours):
dMMR tumours with high mutational burden. Upregulation of MYC pathway.
IntClust 7 (n=19 tumours):
SA tumours mostly with lower mutational burden, however representation of mutations in NOTCH1 and HRAS. Copy number aberrations are absent. Down-regulation of interferon pathways. High proportion of endothelial cells and fibroblasts.
IntClust 8 (n=23 tumours):
Mostly SM and SA tumours, low mutational burden but HRAS and ZNF750 mutations. pMMR and many pathways down regulated.
IntClust 9 (n=10 tumours):
Group comprised exclusively of SC-O tumours, pMMR and low tumour burden. However, almost all of them have mutations in TP53 and ZNF750. Upregulation of E2F and G2M checkpoint pathways. Lower immune component. Many copy number aberrations.

For each Exp-Cluster, we run a logistic regression comparing the probability of observing a mutation (from our subset of 84 genes) in the tumours of that Exp-Cluster with the probability of observing that mutation in the rest of the tumours. After multiple test FDR correction, we represented the significant associations in the following plot. [4.4] Which immune and other non -tumor cell types are present in each of these bulk tumors? How does this correlate with tumor purity?
Using EPIC for cell deconvolution, we estimated proportion of different cell types. As the next plot shows, cluster 2 has a high proportion of endothelial cells, cluster 5 (with up-regulation in interferon pathways, see next section) has a high proportion of B cells, CD4+ T cells and macrophages. Cluster 6 has a slightly higher proportion of CD8+ T cells.
[4.5] Which pathways or genes seems differentially expressed between these groups? Could this be confounded by tumor purity or non-tumor cells or is there evidence that they could represent genuine differences between the cancerous or neoplastic cells?
We performed Gene set enrichment analysis on the full expression matrix on the 50 Hallmark Gene sets, and after FDR correction we identified the following enriched pathways in each Exp-Cluster (red means positive normalised enrichment score (NES), and blue negative NES)
With respect to tumour cellularity, we had purity estimates obtained from the ASCAT algorithm on the DNA sample for 159 samples. We must note that this method is far from perfect and it produces several 100% purity values in 35 of the cases. However, it should give a rough idea of the association with our clusters. As the plot below shows, in the case of the purely transcriptomic clusters, only Exp-Cluster 5 is composed of lower purity tumours (although with a non-significant adjusted t-test from a linear model, p-value=0.055). In the case of the MOFA IntClusts, we also see a group with lower tumour purity, IntClust 4, but again a non statistically difference in the average purity. Overall, purity does not seem to impact any of the clusters.
In summary:
Exp-Cluster 1 is characterised by mainly SC-O tumours and a few SC-E, low mutational burden, but selected mutations in TP53, RB1 and ZNF750. Proficient MMR and pathway activation of E2F targets, G2M checkpoint and MYC targets.
Exp-Cluster 2 is characterised by SM and SA subtypes, 70% of the tumours are MMR deficient and 33% and have several overexpressed pathways, such as Bile Acid Metabolism, myogenesis and UV response down.
Exp-Cluster 3 is enriched in SM tumours, with high mutational burden and almost all of them (96%) MMR deficient (several with MLH1 mutations). They have up-regulation of the MYC pathway and down-regulation of many other pathways.
Exp-Cluster 4 is mostly formed by SA tumours, carrying a large number of mutations (81% of them MMR deficient). Up-regulation of many pathways, such as Estrogen response, inflammatory response, MTORC1 signalling and P53.
Exp-Cluster 5 is mostly characterised by SC-E tumours and activation in the interferon gamma and alpha response pathways. It has a high proportion of B cells, CD4+ T cells and macrophages
Exp-Cluster 6 is mainly formed by SM tumours, with low mutational burden and MMR proficient (94%), with down-regulation of most pathways.
Comparing the purely transcriptomic clusters and the integrative clusters, we see some differences, but the integrative clustering is able to identify interesting tumours with unique combination of mutational and expression profiles, such as IntClust 4.
